entries.cadb95895a8c39cfa13dbaf700d5413452e96515: <div sID="gen29647" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Acts.15" sID="Acts.15"/> <div eID="gen29647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29648" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29649" type="x-p"/> Hitherto we have, with a great deal of pleasure, attended the apostles in their glorious travels for the propagating of the gospel in foreign parts, have seen the bounds of the church enlarged by the accession both of Jews and Gentiles to it; and thanks be to that God who always caused them to triumph. We left them, in the close of the foregoing chapter, reposing themselves at Antioch, and edifying the church there with the rehearsal of their experiences, and it is a pity they should ever be otherwise employed; but in this chapter we find other work (not so pleasant) cut out for them. The Christians and ministers are engaged in controversy, and those that should have been now busied in enlarging the dominions of the church have as much as they can do to compose the divisions of it; when they should have been making war upon the devil's kingdom they have much ado to keep the peace in Christ's kingdom. Yet this occurrence and the record of it are of great use to the church, both for warning to us to expect such unhappy discords among Christians, and direction to us what method to take for accommodating them. Here is, I. A controversy raised at Antioch by the judaizing teachers, who would have the believing Gentiles brought under the yoke of circumcision and the ceremonial law, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.1-Acts.15.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. A consultation held with the church at Jerusalem about this matter, and the sending of delegates thither for that purpose, which occasioned the starting of the same question there, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.3-Acts.15.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. III. An account of what passed in the synod that was convened upon this occasion, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.6">ver. 6</reference>. What Peter said, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.7-Acts.15.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. What Paul and Barnabas discoursed of, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.12">ver. 12</reference>. And, lastly, what James proposed for the settling of this matter, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.13-Acts.15.21">ver. 13-21</reference>. IV. The result of this debate, and the circular letter that was written to the Gentile converts, directing them how to govern themselves with respect to Jews, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.22-Acts.15.29">ver. 22-29</reference>. V. The delivering of this determination to the church at Antioch, and the satisfaction it gave them, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.30-Acts.15.35">ver. 30-35</reference>. VI. A second expedition designed by Paul and Barnabas to preach to the Gentiles, in which they quarrelled about their assistant, and separated upon it, one steering one course and the other another, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.36-Acts.15.41">ver. 36-41</reference>.
entries.7f60f068075f6acca1fc4cb5169008bc0f3985ae: <div eID="gen29649" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29648" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Controversy Raised at Antioch; Bigotry of the Jewish Converts.</title> <div sID="gen29650" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And certain men which came down from Judæa taught the brethren, <hi type="italic">and said,</hi> Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved. <hi type="super">2</hi> When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question. <hi type="super">3</hi> And being brought on their way by the church, they passed through Phenice and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles: and they caused great joy unto all the brethren. <hi type="super">4</hi> And when they were come to Jerusalem, they were received of the church, and <hi type="italic">of</hi> the apostles and elders, and they declared all things that God had done with them. <hi type="super">5</hi> But there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command <hi type="italic">them</hi> to keep the law of Moses. <div eID="gen29650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29651" type="x-p"/> Even when things go on very smoothly and pleasantly in a state or in a church, it is folly to be secure, and to think the mountain stands strong and cannot be moved; some uneasiness or other will arise, which is not foreseen, cannot be prevented, but must be prepared for. If ever there was a heaven upon earth, surely it was in the church at Antioch at this time, when there were so many excellent ministers there, and blessed Paul among them, building up that church in her most holy faith. But here we have their peace disturbed, and differences arising. Here is, <div eID="gen29651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29652" type="x-p"/> I. A new doctrine started among them, which occasioned this division, obliging the Gentile converts to submit to circumcision and the ceremonial law, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.1">v. 1</reference>. Many that had been proselytes to the Jewish religion became Christians; and they would have such as were proselyted to the Christian religion to become Jews. <div eID="gen29652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29653" type="x-p"/> 1. The persons that urged this were <hi type="italic">certain men who came down from Judea;</hi> some think such as had been of the Pharisees (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.5">v. 5</reference>), or perhaps of those priests who were <hi type="italic">obedient to the faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.6.7">ch. vi. 7</reference>. They came from Judea, pretending perhaps to be sent by the apostles at Jerusalem, at least to be countenanced by them. Having a design to spread their notions, they came to Antioch, because that was the head-quarters of those that preached to the Gentiles, and the rendezvous of the Gentile converts; and, if they could but make an interest there, this leaven would soon be diffused to all the churches of the Gentiles. They insinuated themselves into an acquaintance with the brethren, pretended to be very glad that they had embraced the Christian faith, and congratulated them on their conversion; but tell them that <hi type="italic">yet one thing they lack,</hi> they must be circumcised. Note, Those that are ever so well taught have need to stand upon their guard that they be not untaught again, or ill taught. <div eID="gen29653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29654" type="x-p"/> 2. The position they laid down, the thesis they gave, was this, that except the Gentiles who turned Christians were <hi type="italic">circumcised after the manner of Moses,</hi> and thereby bound themselves to all the observances of the ceremonial law, <hi type="italic">they could not be saved.</hi> As to this, (1.) Many of the Jews who embraced the faith of Christ, yet continued very <hi type="italic">zealous for the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.21.20">ch. xxi. 20</reference>. They knew it was from God and its authority was sacred, valued it for its antiquity, had been bred up in the observance of it, and it is probable had been often devoutly affected in their attendance on these observances; they therefore kept them up after they were by baptism admitted into the Christian church, kept up the distinction of meats, and used the ceremonial purifyings from ceremonial pollutions, attend the temple service, and celebrated the feasts of the Jews. Herein they were connived at, because the prejudices of education are not to be overcome all at once, and in a few years the mistake would be effectually rectified by the destruction of the temple and the total dissolution of the Jewish church, by which the observance of the Mosaic ritual would become utterly impracticable. But it did not suffice them that they were herein indulged themselves, they must have the Gentile converts brought under the same obligations. Note, There is a strange proneness in us to make our opinion and practice a rule and a law to every body else, to judge of all about us by our standard, and to conclude that because we do well all do wrong that do not just as we do. (2.) Those Jews who believed that Christ was the Messiah, as they could not get clear of their affection to the law, so they could not get clear of the notions they had of the Messiah, that he should set up a temporal kingdom in favour of the Jewish nation, should make this illustrious and victorious; it was a disappointment to them that there was as yet nothing done towards this in the way they expected. But now that they hear the doctrine of Christ is received among the Gentiles, and his kingdom begins to be set up in the midst of them, if they can but persuade those that embrace Christ to embrace the law of Moses too they hope their point will be gained, the Jewish nation will be made as considerable as they can wish, though in another way; and "Therefore by all means let the brethren be pressed to be <hi type="italic">circumcised and keep the law,</hi> and then with our religion our dominion will be extended, and we shall in a little time be able to shake off the Roman yoke; and not only so, but to put it on the necks of our neighbours, and so shall have such a kingdom of the Messiah as we promised ourselves." Note, It is no wonder if those who have wrong notions of the kingdom of Christ take wrong measures for the advancement of it, and such as really tend to the destruction of it, as these do. (3.) The controversy about the circumcising of the Gentile proselytes had been on foot among the Jews long before this. This is observed by Dr. Whitby out of Josephus—<hi type="italic">Antiq.</hi> 20. 38-45: "That when Izates, the son of Helen queen of Adiabene, embraced the Jews' religion, Ananias declared he might do it without circumcision; but Eleazar maintained that it was a great impiety to remain uncircumcised." And when two eminent Gentiles fled to Josephus (as he relates in the history of his own life) "the zealots among the Jews were urgent for their circumcision; but Josephus dissuaded them from insisting upon it." Such has been the difference in all ages between bigotry and moderation. (4.) It is observable what a mighty stress they laid upon it; they do not only say, "<hi type="italic">You ought to be circumcised after the manner of Moses,</hi> and it will be good service to the kingdom of the Messiah if you be; it will best accommodate matters between you and the Jewish converts, and we shall take it very kindly if you will, and shall converse the more familiarly with you;" but, "<hi type="italic">Except you be circumcised you cannot be saved.</hi> If you be not herein of our mind and way, you will never go to heaven, and therefore of course you must go to hell." Note, it is common for proud impostors to enforce their own inventions under pain of damnation; and to tell people that unless they believe just as they would have them believe, and do just as they would have them do, they cannot be saved, it is impossible they should; not only their case is hazardous, but it is desperate. Thus the Jews tell their brethren that except they be of their church, and come into their communion, and conform to the ceremonies of their worship, though otherwise good men and believers in Christ, yet they cannot be saved; salvation itself cannot save them. None are in Christ but those that are within their pale. We ought to see ourselves well warranted by the word of God before we say, "Except you do so and so, you cannot be saved." <div eID="gen29654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29655" type="x-p"/> II. The opposition which Paul and Barnabas gave to this schismatical notion, which engrossed salvation to the Jews, now that Christ has opened the door of salvation to the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">They had no small dissension and disputation with them.</hi> They would by no means yield to this doctrine, but appeared and argued publicly against it. 1. As faithful servants of Christ, they would not see his truths betrayed. They knew that Christ came to free us from the yoke of the ceremonial law, and to take down that wall of partition between Jews and Gentiles and unite them both in himself; and therefore could not bear to hear of circumcising the Gentile converts, when their instructions were only to baptize them. The Jews would unite with the Gentiles, that is, they would have them to conform in every thing to their rites, and then, and not till then they will look upon them as their brethren; and no thanks to them. But, this not being the way in which Christ designed to unite them, it is not to be admitted. 2. As spiritual fathers to the Gentile converts, they would not see their liberties encroached upon. They had told the Gentiles that if they believed in Jesus Christ they should be saved; and now to be told that this was not enough to save them, except they were circumcised and kept the law of Moses, this was such a discouragement to them at setting out, and would be such a stumbling-block in their way, as might almost tempt them to think of returning into Egypt again; and therefore the apostles set themselves against it. <div eID="gen29655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29656" type="x-p"/> III. The expedient pitched upon for preventing the mischief of this dangerous notion, and silencing those that vented it, as well as quieting the minds of the people with reference to it. They determined that Paul and Barnabas, and some others of their number, should <hi type="italic">go to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders,</hi> concerning this doubt. Not that the church at Antioch had any doubt concerning it: they knew the liberty wherewith Christ had made them free; but they sent the case to Jerusalem, 1. Because those who taught this doctrine came from Jerusalem, and pretended to have directions from the apostles there to urge circumcision upon the Gentile converts; it was therefore very proper to send to Jerusalem about it, to know if they had any such direction from the church there. And it was soon found to be all wrong, which yet pretended to be of apostolical right. It was true that these <hi type="italic">went out from them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.24">v. 24</reference>), but they never had any such orders from them. 2. Because those who were taught this doctrine would be the better confirmed in their opposition to it, and in the less danger of being shocked and disturbed by it, if they were sure that <hi type="italic">the apostles and elders at Jerusalem</hi> (which was the Christian church that of all others retained the most affection to the law of Moses) were against it; and, if they could but have this under their hands, it would be the likeliest means to silence and shame these incendiaries, who had pretended to have it from them. 3. Because the apostles at Jerusalem were fittest to be consulted in a point not yet fully settled; and being most eminent for an infallible spirit, peculiar to them as apostles, their decision would be likely to end the controversy. It was owing to the subtlety and malice of the great enemy of the church's peace (as it appears by Paul's frequent complaints of these <hi type="italic">judaizing teachers,</hi> these <hi type="italic">false apostles,</hi> these <hi type="italic">deceitful workers,</hi> these <hi type="italic">enemies of the cross of Christ</hi>), that it had not this effect. <div eID="gen29656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29657" type="x-p"/> IV. Their journey to Jerusalem upon this errand, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.3">v. 3</reference>. Where we find, 1. That they were honoured at parting: <hi type="italic">They were brought on their way by the church,</hi> which was then much used as a token of respect to useful men, and is directed to be done <hi type="italic">after a godly sort,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.6">3 John 6</reference>. Thus the church showed their favour to those who witnessed against these encroachments on the liberties of the Gentile converts, and stood up for them. 2. That they did good as they went along. They were men that would not lose time, and therefore visited the churches by the way; they passed through Phenice and Samaria, and as they went <hi type="italic">declared the conversion of the Gentiles,</hi> and what wonderful success the gospel had had among them, which <hi type="italic">caused great joy to all the brethren.</hi> Note, The progress of the gospel is and ought to be a matter of great joy. <hi type="italic">All the brethren,</hi> the faithful brethren in Christ's family, rejoice when more are born into the family; for the family will be never the poorer for the multitude of its children. In Christ and heaven there is portion enough, and inheritance enough for them all. <div eID="gen29657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29658" type="x-p"/> V. Their hearty welcome at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.4">v. 4</reference>. 1. The good entertainment their friends gave them: They were <hi type="italic">received of the church, and of the apostles and elders,</hi> were embraced as brethren, and had audience as messengers of the church at Antioch; they received them with all possible expressions of love and friendship. 2. The good entertainment they gave their friends: They <hi type="italic">declared all things that God had done with them,</hi> gave them an account of the success of their ministry among the Gentiles, not what they had done, but <hi type="italic">what God had done with them,</hi> what he had by his grace in them enabled them to do, and what he had by his grace in their hearers enabled them to receive. As they went they had planted, as they came back they had watered; but in both they were ready to own it was God that gave the increase. Note, It is a great honour to be employed for God, to be workers for him; for those that are so have him a worker with them, and he must have all the glory. <div eID="gen29658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29659" type="x-p"/> VI. The opposition they met with from the same party at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.5">v. 5</reference>. When Barnabas and Paul gave an account of the multitude of the Gentiles, and of the great harvest of souls gathered in to Christ there, and all about them congratulated them upon it, <hi type="italic">there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees,</hi> who received the tidings very coldly, and, though they believed in Christ, yet were not satisfied in the admission of these converts, but thought it was needful to circumcise them. Observe here, 1. That those who have been most prejudiced against the gospel yet have been captivated by it; so mighty has it been through God to the pulling down of strong-holds. When Christ was here upon earth, few or none of the rulers and of the Pharisees believed on him; but now there are those of the sect of the Pharisees who believed, and many of them, we hope, in sincerity. 2. That it is very hard for men suddenly to get clear of their prejudices: those that had been Pharisees, even after they became Christians, retained some of the old leaven. All did not so, witness Paul, but some did; and they had such a jealousy for the ceremonial law, and such a dislike of the Gentiles, that they could not admit the Gentiles into communion with them, unless they would be circumcised, and thereby engage themselves to keep the law of Moses. This was, in their opinion, needful; and for their parts they would not converse with them unless they submitted to it.
entries.5b5872025168ae25244120b71dfc3ec66e4b79b8: <div eID="gen29659" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Council at Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen29660" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up, and said unto them, Men <hi type="italic">and</hi> brethren, ye know how that a good while ago God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel, and believe. <hi type="super">8</hi> And God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, giving them the Holy Ghost, even as <hi type="italic">he did</hi> unto us; <hi type="super">9</hi> And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith. <hi type="super">10</hi> Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? <hi type="super">11</hi> But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then all the multitude kept silence, and gave audience to Barnabas and Paul, declaring what miracles and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles by them. <hi type="super">13</hi> And after they had held their peace, James answered, saying, Men <hi type="italic">and</hi> brethren, hearken unto me: <hi type="super">14</hi> Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name. <hi type="super">15</hi> And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written, <hi type="super">16</hi> After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down; and I will build again the ruins thereof, and I will set it up: <hi type="super">17</hi> That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called, saith the Lord, who doeth all these things. <hi type="super">18</hi> Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world. <hi type="super">19</hi> Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God: <hi type="super">20</hi> But that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> fornication, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> things strangled, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> blood. <hi type="super">21</hi> For Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath day. <div eID="gen29660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29661" type="x-p"/> We have here a council called, not by writ, but by consent, on this occasion (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The apostles and presbyters came together, to consider this matter.</hi> They did not give their judgment separately, but came together to do it, that they might hear one another's sense in this matter; for in the multitude of counsellors there is safety and satisfaction. They did not give their judgment rashly, but considered of this matter. Though they were clear concerning it in their own minds, yet they would take time to consider of it, and to hear what might be said by the adverse party. Nor did the apostles give their judgment concerning it without the elders, the inferior ministers, to whom they thus condescended, and on whom they thus put an honour. Those that are most eminent in gifts and graces, and are in the most exalted stations in the church, ought to show respect to their juniors and inferiors; for, though <hi type="italic">days should speak,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">there is a spirit in man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.32.7-Job.32.8">Job xxxii. 7, 8</reference>. Here is a direction to the pastors of the churches, when difficulties arise, to come together in solemn meetings for mutual advice and encouragement, that they may know one another's mind, and strengthen one another's hands, and may act in concert. Now here we have, <div eID="gen29661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29662" type="x-p"/> I. Peter's speech in this synod. He did not in the least pretend to any primacy or headship in this synod. He was not master of this assembly, nor so much as chairman or moderator, <hi type="italic">pro hac vice—on this occasion;</hi> for we do not find that either he spoke first, to open the synod (<hi type="italic">there having been much disputing</hi> before he <hi type="italic">rose up</hi>), nor that he spoke last, to sum up the cause and collect the suffrages; but he was a faithful, prudent zealous member of this assembly, and offered that which was very much to the purpose, and which would come better from him than from another, because he had himself been the first that preached the gospel to the Gentiles. <hi type="italic">There had been much disputing, pro and con,</hi> upon this question, and liberty of speech allowed, as ought to be in such cases; those of the sect of the Pharisees were some of them present, and allowed to say what they could in defence of those of their opinion at Antioch, which probably was answered by some of the elders; such questions ought to be fairly disputed before they are decided. When both sides had been heard, <hi type="italic">Peter rose up,</hi> and addressed himself to the assembly, <hi type="italic">Men and brethren,</hi> as did James afterwards, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.13">v. 13</reference>. And here, <div eID="gen29662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29663" type="x-p"/> 1. He put them in mind of the call and commission he had some time ago <hi type="italic">to preach the gospel to the Gentiles;</hi> he wondered there should be any difficulty made of a matter already settled: <hi type="italic">You know that</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aph hemeron archaion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">from the beginning of the days</hi> of the gospel, many years ago, <hi type="italic">God made choice</hi> among us apostles of one to preach the gospel to the Gentiles, and I was the person chosen, <hi type="italic">that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word, and believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.7">v. 7</reference>. You know I was questioned about it and cleared myself to the universal satisfaction; every body rejoiced that <hi type="italic">God had granted to the Gentiles repentance unto life,</hi> and nobody said a word of circumcising them, nor was there any thought of such a thing. See <reference osisRef="Acts.11.18">ch. xi. 18</reference>. "Why should the Gentiles who hear the word of the gospel by Paul's mouth be compelled to submit to circumcision, any more than those that heard it by my mouth? Or why should the terms of their admission now be made harder than they were then?" <div eID="gen29663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29664" type="x-p"/> 2. He puts them in mind how remarkably God owned him in preaching to the Gentiles, and gave testimony to their sincerity in embracing the Christian faith (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">God, who knows the hearts,</hi> and therefore is able to judge infallibly of men, <hi type="italic">bore them witness</hi> that they were his indeed, by <hi type="italic">giving them the Holy Ghost;</hi> not only the graces and comforts, but the extraordinary miraculous gifts of the Holy Ghost, <hi type="italic">even as he did unto us</hi> apostles." See <reference osisRef="Acts.11.15-Acts.11.17">ch. xi. 15-17</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">The Lord knows those that are his,</hi> for he knows men's hearts; and we are as our hearts are. Those to whom God <hi type="italic">gives the Holy Ghost,</hi> he thereby <hi type="italic">bears witness</hi> to that they are his; hence we are said to be <hi type="italic">sealed</hi> with that Holy Spirit of promise—<hi type="italic">marked</hi> for God. God had bidden the Gentiles welcome to the privilege of communion with him, without requiring them to be circumcised and to keep the law; and therefore shall not we admit them into communion with us but upon those terms? "God has <hi type="italic">put no difference between us and them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.9">v. 9</reference>); they, though Gentiles, are as welcome to the grace of Christ and the throne of grace as we Jews are; why then should we set them at a distance, as if we were holier than they?" <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>. Note, We ought not to make any conditions of our brethren's acceptance with us but such as God has made the conditions of their acceptance with him, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.3">Rom. xiv. 3</reference>. Now the Gentiles were fitted for communion with God, in <hi type="italic">having their hearts purified by faith,</hi> and that faith God's own work in them; and therefore why should we think them unfit for communion with us, unless they will submit to the ceremonial purifying enjoined by the law to us? Note, (1.) <hi type="italic">By faith the heart is purified;</hi> we are not only justified, and conscience purified, but the work of sanctification is begun and carried on. (2.) Those that have their hearts purified by faith are therein made so nearly to resemble one another, that, whatever difference there may be between them, no account is to be made of it; for the faith of all the saints is alike precious, and has like precious effects (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.1">2 Peter i. 1</reference>), and those that by it are united to Christ are so to look upon themselves as joined to one another as that all distinctions, even that between Jew and Gentile, are merged and swallowed up in it. <div eID="gen29664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29665" type="x-p"/> 3. He sharply reproves those teachers (some of whom, it is likely, were present) who went about to bring the Gentiles under the obligation of the law of Moses, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.10">v. 10</reference>. The thing is so plain that he cannot forbear speaking of it with some warmth: "<hi type="italic">Now therefore,</hi> since God has owned them for his, <hi type="italic">why tempt you God to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples,</hi> of the believing Gentiles and their children" (for circumcision was a yoke upon their infant seed, who are here reckoned among the disciples), "<hi type="italic">a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?</hi>" Here he shows that in this attempt, (1.) They offered a very great affront to God: "You tempt him, by calling that in question which he has already settled and determined by no less an indication than that of the gift of the Holy Ghost; you do, in effect, ask, 'Did he know what he did? Or was he in earnest in it? Or will he abide by his own act?' Will you try whether God, who designed the ceremonial law for the people of the Jews only, will now, in its last ages, bring the Gentiles too under the obligation of it, to gratify you?" Those tempt God who prescribe to him, and say that people cannot be saved but upon such and such terms, which God never appointed; as if the God of salvation must come into their measures. (2.) They offered a very great wrong to the disciples: Christ came to proclaim <hi type="italic">liberty to the captives,</hi> and they go about to enslave those whom he has made free. See <reference osisRef="Neh.5.8">Neh. v. 8</reference>. The ceremonial law was a heavy yoke; they and their fathers found it difficult to be borne, so numerous, so various, so pompous, were the institutions of it. The distinction of meats was a heavy yoke, not only as it rendered conversation less pleasant, but as it embarrassed conscience with endless scruples. The ado that was made about even unavoidable touch of a grave or a dead body, the pollution contracted by it, and the many rules about purifying from that pollution, were a heavy burden. This yoke Christ came to ease us of, and called those that were <hi type="italic">weary and heavy laden</hi> under it to come and take his yoke upon them, his easy yoke. Now for these teachers to go about to lay that yoke upon the neck of the Gentiles from which he came to free even the Jews was the greatest injury imaginable to them. <div eID="gen29665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29666" type="x-p"/> 4. Whereas the Jewish teachers had urged that circumcision was necessary to salvation, Peter shows it was so far from being so that both Jews and Gentiles were to be saved purely <hi type="italic">through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> and in no other way (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">We believe to be saved through that grace</hi> only; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pisteuomen sothenai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">We hope to be saved;</hi> or, <hi type="italic">We believe unto salvation in the same manner as they</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kath hontropon kakeinoi.</hi></hi> "We that are circumcised believe to salvation, and so do those that are uncircumcised; and, as our circumcision will be no advantage to us, so their uncircumcision will be no disadvantage to them; for we must depend upon the grace of Christ for salvation, and must apply that grace by faith, as well as they. There is not one way of salvation for the Jews and another for the Gentiles; <hi type="italic">neither circumcision avails any thing nor uncircumcision</hi> (that is neither here nor there), <hi type="italic">but faith which works by love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Gal. v. 6</reference>. Why should we burden them with the law of Moses, as necessary to their salvation, when it is not that, but the gospel of Christ, that is necessary both to our salvation and theirs?" <div eID="gen29666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29667" type="x-p"/> II. An account of what Barnabas and Paul said in this synod, which did not need to be related, for they only gave in a narrative of what was recorded in the foregoing chapters, <hi type="italic">what miracles and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles by them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.12">v. 12</reference>. This they had given in to the church <hi type="italic">at Antioch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.27">ch. xiv. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">to their brethren by the way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.3">ch. xv. 3</reference>), and now again to the synod; and it was very proper to be given in here. That which was contended for was that the Gentiles ought to submit to the law of Moses; now, in opposition to this, Paul and Barnabas undertake to show, by a plain relation of matters of fact, that God owned the preaching of the pure gospel to them without the law, and therefore to press the law upon them now was to undo what God had done. Observe, 1. What account they gave; they declared, or opened in order, and with all the magnifying and affecting circumstances, what glorious miracles, what signs and wonders, <hi type="italic">God had wrought among the Gentiles by them,</hi> what confirmation he had given to their preaching by miracles wrought in the kingdom of nature, and what success he had given to it by miracles wrought in the kingdom of grace. Thus God had honoured these apostles whom Jewish teachers condemned, and had thus honoured the Gentiles whom they contemned. What need had they of any other advocate when God himself pleaded their cause? The conversion of the Gentiles was itself a wonder, all things considered, no less than a miracle. Now if <hi type="italic">they received the Holy Ghost by the hearing of faith,</hi> why should they be embarrassed with <hi type="italic">the works of the law?</hi> See <reference osisRef="Gal.3.2">Gal. iii. 2</reference>. 2. What attention was given to them: <hi type="italic">All the multitude</hi> (who, though they had not voted, yet came together to hear what was said) <hi type="italic">kept silence, and gave audience to Paul and Barnabas;</hi> it should seem they took more notice of their narrative than they did of all the arguments that were offered. As in natural philosophy and medicine nothing is so satisfactory as experiments, and in law nothing is so satisfactory as cases adjudged, so in the things of God the best explication of the word of grace is the accounts given of the operations of the Spirit of grace; to these the multitude will with silence give audience. Those that fear God will most readily hear those that can tell them <hi type="italic">what God has done for their souls,</hi> or by their means, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen29667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29668" type="x-p"/> III. The speech which James made to the synod. He did not interrupt Paul and Barnabas, though, it is likely, he had before heard their narrative, but let them go on with it, for the edification of the company, and that they might have it from the first and best hand; but, <hi type="italic">after they had held their peace,</hi> then James stood up. <hi type="italic">You may all prophesy one by one,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.31">1 Cor. xiv. 31</reference>. God is the God of order. He let Paul and Barnabas say what they had to say, and then he made the application of it. The hearing of variety of ministers may be of use when one truth does not drive out, but clench, another. <div eID="gen29668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29669" type="x-p"/> 1. He addresses himself respectfully to those present: "<hi type="italic">Men and brethren, hearken unto me.</hi> You are men, and therefore, it is to be hoped, will hear reason; you are my brethren, and therefore will hear me with candour. We are all brethren, and equally concerned in this cause that nothing be done to the dishonour of Christ and the uneasiness of Christians." <div eID="gen29669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29670" type="x-p"/> 2. He refers to what Peter had said concerning the conversion of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Simeon</hi>" (that is, Simon Peter) "<hi type="italic">hath declared,</hi> and opened the matter to you—<hi type="italic">how God at the first did visit the Gentiles,</hi> in Cornelius and his friends, who were the first-fruits of the Gentiles—how, when the gospel began first to spread, presently the Gentiles were invited to come and take the benefit of it;" and James observes here, (1.) That the <hi type="italic">grace of God</hi> was the origin of it; it was God <hi type="italic">that visited the Gentiles;</hi> and it was a kind visit. Had they been left to themselves, they would never have visited him, but the acquaintance began on his part; he not only <hi type="italic">visited and redeemed his people,</hi> but visited and redeemed those that were <hi type="italic">lo ammi—not a people.</hi> (2.) that the glory of God was the end of it: it was <hi type="italic">to take out of them a people for his name,</hi> who should glorify him, and in whom he would be glorified. As of old he took the Jews, so now the Gentiles, <hi type="italic">to be to him for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>. Let all the people of God remember that therefore they are thus dignified in God, that God may be glorified in them. <div eID="gen29670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29671" type="x-p"/> 3. He confirms this with a quotation out of the Old Testament: he could not prove the calling of the Gentiles by a vision, as Peter could, nor by miracles wrought by his hand, as Paul and Barnabas could, but he would prove that it was foretold in the Old Testament, and therefore it must be fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.15">v. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">To this agree the words of the prophets;</hi> most of the Old-Testament prophets spoke more or less of the calling in of the Gentiles, even Moses himself, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.19">Rom. x. 19</reference>. It was the general expectation of the pious Jews that the Messiah should be <hi type="italic">a light to enlighten the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Luke ii. 32</reference>): but James waives the more illustrious prophecies of this, and pitches upon one that seemed more obscure: <hi type="italic">It is written,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.9.11-Amos.9.12">Amos ix. 11, 12</reference>, where is foretold, (1.) The setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will raise up the tabernacle of David, that is fallen.</hi> The covenant was made with David and his seed; but the house and family of David are here called his <hi type="italic">tabernacle,</hi> because David in his beginning was a shepherd, and dwelt in tents, and his house, that had been as a stately palace, had become a mean and despicable tabernacle, reduced in a manner to its small beginning. This tabernacle was ruined and <hi type="italic">fallen down;</hi> there had not been for many ages a king of the house of David; <hi type="italic">the sceptre had departed from Judah,</hi> the royal family was sunk and buried in obscurity, and, as it should seem, not enquired after. But God <hi type="italic">will return, and will build it again,</hi> raise it out of its ruins, a phoenix out of its ashes; and this was now lately fulfilled, when our Lord Jesus was raised out of that family, had <hi type="italic">the throne of his father David given him,</hi> with a promise <hi type="italic">that he should reign over the house of Jacob for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32-Luke.1.33">Luke i. 32, 33</reference>. And, when <hi type="italic">the tabernacle of David</hi> was thus rebuilt in Christ, all the rest of it was, not many years after, wholly extirpated and cut off, as was also the nation of the Jews itself, and all their genealogies were lost. The church of Christ may be called the tabernacle of David. This may sometimes be brought very low, and may seem to be in ruins, but it shall be built again, its withering interests shall revive; it is <hi type="italic">cast down, but not destroyed:</hi> even dry bones are made to live. (2.) The bringing in of the Gentiles as the effect and consequence of this (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">That the residue of men might seek after the Lord;</hi> not the Jews only, who thought they had the monopoly of the tabernacle of David, but <hi type="italic">the residue of men,</hi> such as had hitherto been left out of the pale of the visible church; they must now, upon this re-edifying of the tabernacle of David, be brought <hi type="italic">to seek after the Lord,</hi> and to enquire how they may obtain his favour. When David's tabernacle is set up, they <hi type="italic">shall seek the Lord their God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">David their king,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jer. xxx. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then Israel shall possess the remnant of Edom</hi> (so it is in the Hebrew); but the Jews called all the Gentiles <hi type="italic">Edomites,</hi> and therefore the Septuagint leave out the particular mention of Edom, and read it just as it is here, <hi type="italic">that the residue of men might seek</hi> (James here adds, <hi type="italic">after the Lord), and all the Gentiles,</hi> or heathen, <hi type="italic">upon whom my name is called.</hi> The Jews were for many ages so peculiarly favoured that the residue of men seemed neglected; but now God will have an eye to them, and his name shall be called upon by the Gentiles; his name shall be declared and published among them, and they shall be brought both to know his name and to call upon it: they shall call themselves the people of God, and he shall call them so; and thus, by consent of both parties, <hi type="italic">his name is called upon them.</hi> This promise we may depend upon the fulfilling of in its season; and now it begins to be fulfilled, for it is added, <hi type="italic">saith the Lord, who doeth this; who doeth all these things</hi> (so the Seventy); and the apostle here: <hi type="italic">he saith it who doeth it,</hi> who therefore said it because he was determined to do it; and who therefore does it because he hath said it; for though with us saying and doing are two things they are not so with God. The uniting of <hi type="italic">Jews and Gentiles in one body,</hi> and all those things that were done in order to it, which were here foretold, were, [1.] What God did: <hi type="italic">This was the Lord's doing,</hi> whatever instruments were employed in it: and, [2.] It was what God delighted in, and was well pleased with; for he is the God of the Gentiles, as well as the Jews, and it is his honour <hi type="italic">to be rich in mercy to all that call upon him.</hi> <div eID="gen29671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29672" type="x-p"/> 4. He resolves it into the purpose and counsel of God (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.</hi> He not only foretold the calling of the Gentiles many ages ago by the prophets (and therefore it ought not to be a surprise or stumbling-block to us), but he foresaw and foreordained it in his eternal counsels, which are unquestionably wise and unalterably firm. It is an excellent maxim here laid down concerning all God's works, both of providence and grace, in the natural and spiritual kingdom, that they were all <hi type="italic">known unto him from the beginning of the world,</hi> from the time he first began to work, which supposes his knowing them (as other scriptures speak) <hi type="italic">from before the foundation of the world,</hi> and therefore from all eternity. Note, Whatever God does, he did before design and determine to do; for he works all, not only according to his will, but <hi type="italic">according to the counsel of his will:</hi> he not only <hi type="italic">does whatever he determined</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.6">Ps. cxxxv. 6</reference>), which is more than we can do (our purposes are frequently broken off, and our measures broken), but he <hi type="italic">determined whatever he does.</hi> Whatever he may say, to prove us, <hi type="italic">he himself knows what he will do.</hi> We know not our works beforehand, but must <hi type="italic">do as occasion shall serve,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7">1 Sam. x. 7</reference>. What we shall do in such or such a case we cannot tell till it comes to the setting to; but <hi type="italic">known unto God are all his works;</hi> in the volume of his book (called <hi type="italic">the scriptures of truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">Dan. x. 21</reference>) they are all written in order, without any erasure or interlining (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Ps. xl. 7</reference>); and all God's works will, in the day of review, be found to agree exactly with his counsels, without the least error or variation. We are poor short-sighted creatures; the wisest men can see but a little way before them, and not at all with any certainty; but this is our comfort, that, whatever uncertainty we are at, there is an infallible certainty in the divine prescience: <hi type="italic">known unto God are all his works.</hi> <div eID="gen29672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29673" type="x-p"/> 5. He gives his advice what was to be done in the present case, as the matter now stood with reference <hi type="italic">to the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">My sentence is;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ego krino</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I give it as my opinion,</hi> or judgment; not as having authority over the rest, but as being an adviser with them. Now his advice is, <div eID="gen29673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29674" type="x-p"/> (1.) That circumcision and the observance of the ceremonial law be by no means imposed upon the Gentile converts; no, not so much as recommended nor mentioned to them. "There are many from among the Gentiles that are turned to God in Christ, and we hope there will be many more. Now I am clearly for using them with all possible tenderness, and putting no manner of hardship or discouragement upon them," <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me parenochlein</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">not to give them any molestation nor disturbance,</hi> nor suggest any thing to them that may be disquieting, or raise scruples in their minds, or perplex them." Note, Great care must be taken not to discourage nor disquiet young converts with matters of <hi type="italic">doubtful disputation.</hi> Let the essentials of religion, which an awakened conscience will readily receive, be first impressed deeply upon them, and these will satisfy them and make them easy; and let not things foreign and circumstantial be urged upon them, which will but trouble them. <hi type="italic">The kingdom of God,</hi> in which they are to be trained up, <hi type="italic">is not meat and drink,</hi> neither the opposition nor the imposition of indifferent things, which will but trouble them; <hi type="italic">but it is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost,</hi> which we are sure will trouble nobody. <div eID="gen29674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29675" type="x-p"/> (2.) That yet it would be well that in some things, which gave most offence to the Jews, the Gentiles should comply with them. Because they must not humour them so far as to be circumcised, and keep the whole law, it does not therefore follow that they must act in a continual contradiction to them, and study how to provoke them. It will please the Jews (and, if a little thing will oblige them, better do so than cross them) if the Gentile converts abstain, [1.] <hi type="italic">From pollutions of idols, and from fornication,</hi> which are two bad things, and always to be abstained from; but writing to them particularly and expressly to abstain from them (because in these things the Jews were jealous of the Gentile converts, lest they should transgress) would very much gratify the Jews; not but that the apostles, both in preaching and writing to the Gentiles that embraced Christianity, were careful to warn against, <hi type="italic">First, Pollutions of idols,</hi> that they should have no manner of fellowship with idolaters in their idolatrous worships, and particularly not in the feasts they held upon their sacrifices. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.14 2Cor.6.14">1 Cor. x. 14, &c.; 2 Cor. vi. 14</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Fornication, and all manner of uncleanness.</hi> How large, how pressing, is Paul in his cautions against this sin! <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.9-1Cor.6.15">1 Cor. vi. 9-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Eph. v. 3</reference>, &c. But the Jews, who were willing to think the worst of those they did not like, suggested that these were things in which the Gentiles, even after conversion, allowed themselves, and the apostle of the Gentiles connived at it. Now, to obviate this suggestion, and to leave no room for this calumny, James advises that, besides the private admonitions which were given them by their ministers, they should be publicly warned <hi type="italic">to abstain from pollutions of idols and from fornication</hi>—that herein they should be very circumspect, and should avoid all appearances of these two evils, which would be in so particular a manner offensive to the Jews. [2.] <hi type="italic">From things strangled, and from blood,</hi> which, though not evil in themselves, as the other two, nor designed to be always abstained from, as those were, had been forbidden by <hi type="italic">the precepts of Noah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen. ix. 4</reference>), before the giving of the law of Moses; and the Jews had a great dislike to them, and to all those that took a liberty to use them; and therefore, to avoid giving offence, let the Gentile converts abridge themselves of their liberty herein, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">1 Cor. viii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.13">13</reference>. Thus we must <hi type="italic">become all things to all men.</hi> <div eID="gen29675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29676" type="x-p"/> 6. He gives a reason for his advice—that great respect ought to be shown to the Jews for they have been so long accustomed to the solemn injunctions of the ceremonial law that they must be borne with, if they cannot presently come off from them (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">For Moses hath of old those that preach him in every city,</hi> his writings (a considerable part of which is the ceremonial law) <hi type="italic">being read in the synagogues every sabbath day.</hi> "You cannot blame them if they have a great veneration for the law of Moses; for besides that they are very sure God spoke to Moses," (1.) "Moses is continually preached to them, and they are called upon <hi type="italic">to remember the law of Moses,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mal.4.4">Mal. iv. 4</reference>. Note, Even that word of God which is written to us should also be preached: those that have the scriptures have still need of ministers to help them to understand and apply the scriptures. (2.) "His writings are read in a solemn religious manner, <hi type="italic">in their synagogues,</hi> and on <hi type="italic">the sabbath day,</hi> in the place and at the time of their meetings for the worship of God; so that from their childhood they have been trained up in a regard to the law of Moses; the observance of it is a part of their religion." (3.) "This has been done <hi type="italic">of old time;</hi> they have received from their fathers an honour for Moses; they have antiquity for it." (4.) "This had been done <hi type="italic">in every city,</hi> wherever there are any Jews, so that none of them can be ignorant what stress that law laid upon these things: and therefore, though the gospel has set us free from these things, yet they cannot be blamed if they are loth to part with them, and cannot of a sudden be persuaded to look upon those things as needless and indifferent which they, and their fathers before them, had been so long taught, and taught of God too, to place religion in. We must therefore give them time, must meet them half-way; they must be borne with awhile, and brought on gradually, and we must comply with them as far as we can without betraying our gospel liberty." Thus does this apostle show the spirit of a moderator, that is, a spirit of moderation, being careful to give no offence either to Jew or Gentile, and contriving, as much as may be, to please both sides and provoke neither. Note, We are not to think it strange if people be wedded to customs which they have had transmitted to them from their fathers, and which they have been educated in an opinion of as sacred; and therefore allowances must be made in such cases, and not rigour used.
entries.9ee620026e483b51c0b7d1798a4af016ba161f23: <div eID="gen29676" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Decision of the Council at Jerusalem; The Publication of the Decree.</title> <div sID="gen29677" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren: <hi type="super">23</hi> And they wrote <hi type="italic">letters</hi> by them after this manner; The apostles and elders and brethren <hi type="italic">send</hi> greeting unto the brethren which are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia: <hi type="super">24</hi> Forasmuch as we have heard, that certain which went out from us have troubled you with words, subverting your souls, saying, <hi type="italic">Ye must</hi> be circumcised, and keep the law: to whom we gave no <hi type="italic">such</hi> commandment: <hi type="super">25</hi> It seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men unto you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, <hi type="super">26</hi> Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. <hi type="super">27</hi> We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who shall also tell <hi type="italic">you</hi> the same things by mouth. <hi type="super">28</hi> For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things; <hi type="super">29</hi> That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well. <hi type="super">30</hi> So when they were dismissed, they came to Antioch: and when they had gathered the multitude together, they delivered the epistle: 31 <hi type="italic">Which</hi> when they had read, they rejoiced for the consolation. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Judas and Silas, being prophets also themselves, exhorted the brethren with many words, and confirmed <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">33</hi> And after they had tarried <hi type="italic">there</hi> a space, they were let go in peace from the brethren unto the apostles. <hi type="super">34</hi> Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still. <hi type="super">35</hi> Paul also and Barnabas continued in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. <div eID="gen29677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29678" type="x-p"/> We have here the result of the consultation that was held at Jerusalem about the imposing of the ceremonial law upon the Gentiles. Much more, it is likely, was said about it than is here recorded; but at length it was brought to a head, and the advice which James gave was universally approved and agreed to <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente—unanimously;</hi> and letters were accordingly sent by messengers of their own to the Gentile converts, acquainting them with their sentiments in this matter, which would be a great confirmation to them against the false teachers. Now observe here, <div eID="gen29678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29679" type="x-p"/> I. The choice of the delegates that were to be sent with Paul and Barnabas on this errand; not as if they had any suspicion of the fidelity of these great men, and could not trust them with their letters, nor as if they thought that those to whom they sent them would suspect them to have altered any thing in their letter; no, their charity thought no such evil concerning men of such tried integrity; but, <div eID="gen29679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29680" type="x-p"/> 1. They thought fit <hi type="italic">to send men of their own company to Antioch, with Paul and Barnabas,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.22">v. 22</reference>. This was agreed to by <hi type="italic">the apostles and elders, with the whole church,</hi> who, it is likely, undertook to bear their charges, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. They sent these messengers, (1.) To show their respect to the church at Antioch, as a sister-church, though a younger sister, and that they looked upon it as upon the same level with them; as also that they were desirous further to know their state. (2.) To encourage Paul and Barnabas, and to make their journey home the more pleasant (for it is likely they travelled on foot) by sending such excellent men to bear them company; <hi type="italic">amicus pro vehiculo—a friend instead of a carriage.</hi> (3.) To put a reputation upon the letters they carried, that it might appear a solemn embassy, and so much the more regard might be paid to the message, which was likely to meet with opposition from some. (4.) To keep up <hi type="italic">the communion of the saints,</hi> and cultivate an acquaintance between churches and ministers that were at a distance from each other, and to show <hi type="italic">that, though they were many, yet they were one.</hi> <div eID="gen29680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29681" type="x-p"/> 2. Those they sent were not inferior persons, who might serve to carry the letters, and attest the receipt of them from the apostles; but <hi type="italic">they were chosen men, and chief men among the brethren,</hi> men of eminent gifts, graces, and usefulness; for these are the things which denominate men chief among the brethren, and qualify them to be the messengers of the churches. They are here named: <hi type="italic">Judas,</hi> who was called <hi type="italic">Barsabas</hi> (probably the brother of that Joseph who was called <hi type="italic">Barsabas,</hi> that was a candidate for the apostleship, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.23">ch. i. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">and Silas.</hi> The character which these men had in the church at Jerusalem would have some influence upon those that came from Judea, as those false teachers did, and engage them to pay the more deference to the message that was sent by them. <div eID="gen29681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29682" type="x-p"/> II. The drawing up of the letters, circular letters, that were to be sent to the churches, to notify the sense of the synod in this matter. <div eID="gen29682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29683" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is a very condescending obliging preamble to this decree, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.23">v. 23</reference>. There is nothing in it haughty or assuming, but, (1.) That which intimates the humility of the apostles, that they join <hi type="italic">the elders and brethren</hi> in commission with them, the ministers, the ordinary Christians, whom they had advised with in this case, as they used to do in other cases. Though never men were so qualified as they were for a monarchical power and authority in the church, nor had such a commission as they had, yet their decrees run not, "We, the apostles, Christ's vicars upon earth, and pastors of all the pastors of the churches" (as the pope styles himself), "and sole judges in all matters of faith;" but <hi type="italic">the apostles, and elders, and brethren,</hi> agree in their orders. Herein they remembered the instructions their Master gave them (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.8">Matt. xxiii. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be not you called Rabbi; for you are all brethren.</hi> (2.) That which bespeaks their respect to the churches they wrote to; they <hi type="italic">send</hi> to them <hi type="italic">greeting,</hi> wish them health and happiness and joy, and call them <hi type="italic">brethren of the Gentiles,</hi> thereby owning their admission into the church, and giving them the right hand of fellowship: "You are our brethren, though Gentiles; for we meet in Christ, <hi type="italic">the first born among many brethren,</hi> in God our common Father." Now that <hi type="italic">the Gentiles are fellow-heirs and of the same body,</hi> they are to be countenanced and encouraged, and called brethren. <div eID="gen29683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29684" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is a just and severe rebuke to the judaizing teachers (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.24">v. 24</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We have heard that certain who went out from us have troubled you with words,</hi> and we are very much concerned to hear it; now this is to let them know that those who preached this doctrine were false teachers, both as they produced a false commission and as they taught a false doctrine." (1.) They did a great deal of wrong to the apostles and ministers at Jerusalem, in pretending that they had instructions from them to impose the ceremonial law upon the Gentiles, when there was no colour for such a pretension. "They <hi type="italic">went out from us</hi> indeed—they were such as belonged to our church, of which, when they had a mind to travel, we gave them perhaps a testimonial; but, as for their urging the law of Moses upon you, we <hi type="italic">gave</hi> them <hi type="italic">no such commandment,</hi> nor had we ever thought of such a thing, nor given them the least occasion to use our names in it." It is no new thing for apostolical authority to be pleaded in defence of those doctrines and practices for which yet the apostles gave neither command nor encouragement. (2.) They did a great deal of wrong to the Gentile converts, in saying, <hi type="italic">You must be circumcised, and must keep the law.</hi> [1.] It perplexed them: "<hi type="italic">They have troubled you with words,</hi> have occasioned disturbance and disquietment to you. You depended upon those who told you, <hi type="italic">If you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ you shall be saved;</hi> and now you are startled by those that tell you <hi type="italic">you must keep the law of Moses or you cannot be saved,</hi> by which you see yourselves drawn into a snare. They trouble you with words—words, and nothing else—mere words—sound, but no substance." How has the church been troubled with words, by the pride of men that loved to hear themselves talk! [2.] It endangered them; they <hi type="italic">subverted</hi> their souls, put them into disorder, and pulled down that which had been built up. They took them off from pursuing pure Christianity, and minding the business of that, by filling their heads with the necessity of circumcision, and the law of Moses, which were nothing to the purpose. <div eID="gen29684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29685" type="x-p"/> 3. Here is an honourable testimony given of the messengers by whom these letters were sent. <div eID="gen29685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29686" type="x-p"/> (1.) Of Paul and Barnabas, whom these judaizing teachers had opposed and censured as having done their work by the halves, because they had brought the Gentile converts to Christianity only, and not to Judaism. Let them say what they will of these men, [1.] "They are men that are dear to us; they are <hi type="italic">our beloved Barnabas and Paul</hi>—men whom we have a value for, a kindness for, a concern for." Sometimes it is good for those that are of eminence to express their esteem, not only for the despised truth of Christ, but for the despised preachers and defenders of that truth, to encourage them, and weaken the hands of their opposers. [2.] "They are men that have signalized themselves in the service of Christ, and therefore have deserved well of all the churches: they are men <hi type="italic">that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.26">v. 26</reference>), and therefore are worthy of double honour, and cannot be suspected of having sought any secular advantage to themselves; for they have ventured their all for Christ, have engaged in the most dangerous services, as good soldiers of Christ, and not only in laborious services." It is not likely that such faithful confessors should be unfaithful preachers. Those that urged circumcision did it to avoid persecution (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.12-Gal.6.13">Gal. vi. 12, 13</reference>); those that opposed it knew they thereby exposed themselves to persecution; and which of these were most likely to be in the right? <div eID="gen29686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29687" type="x-p"/> (2.) Of Judas and Silas: "<hi type="italic">They are chosen men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.25">v. 25</reference>), and they are men that have heard our debates, and are perfectly apprized of the matter, and will <hi type="italic">tell you the same things by mouth,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Acts.15.27">v. 27</reference>. What is of use to us it is good to have both in writing and by word of mouth, that we may have the advantage both of reading and of hearing it. The apostles refer them to the bearers for a further account of their judgment and their reasons, and the bearers will refer them to their letters for the certainty of the determination. <div eID="gen29687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29688" type="x-p"/> 4. Here is the direction given what to require from the Gentile converts, where observe, <div eID="gen29688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29689" type="x-p"/> (1.) The matter of the injunction, which is according to the advice given by James, that, to avoid giving offence to the Jews, [1.] They should never eat any thing that they knew had been offered in sacrifice to an idol, but look upon it as, though clean in itself, yet thereby polluted to them. This prohibition was afterwards in part taken off, for they were allowed to eat whatever was sold in the shambles, or set before them at their friend's table, though it had been offered to idols, except when there was danger of giving offence by it, that is, of giving occasion either to a weak Christian to think the worse of our Christianity, or to a wicked heathen to think the better of his idolatry; and in these cases it is <hi type="italic">good to forbear,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.25">1 Cor. x. 25</reference>, &c. This to us is an antiquated case. [2.] <hi type="italic">That they should not eat blood,</hi> nor drink it; but avoid every thing that looked cruel and barbarous in that ceremony which had been of so long standing. [3.] <hi type="italic">That they should not eat any thing that was strangled,</hi> or died of itself, or had not the blood let out. [4.] That they should be very strict in censuring those that <hi type="italic">were guilty of fornication,</hi> or marrying within the degrees prohibited by the Levitical law, which, some think, is principally intended here. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1 Cor. v. 1</reference>. Dr. Hammond states this matter thus: The judaizing teachers would have the Gentile converts submit to all that those submitted to whom they called the proselytes of righteousness, <hi type="italic">to be circumcised and keep the whole law;</hi> but the apostles required no more of them than what was required of the proselytes of the gate, which was to observe <hi type="italic">the seven precepts of the sons of Noah,</hi> which, he thinks, are here referred to. But the only ground of this decree being in complaisance to the rigid Jews that had embraced the Christian faith, and, except in that one case of scandal, all meats being pronounced free and indifferent to all Christians as soon as the reason of the decree ceased, which, at furthest, was after the destruction of Jerusalem, the obligation of it ceased likewise. "These things are in a particular manner offensive to the Jews, and therefore do not disoblige them herein for the present; in a little time the Jews will incorporate with the Gentiles, and then the danger is over." <div eID="gen29689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29690" type="x-p"/> (2.) The manner in which it is worded. [1.] They express themselves with something of authority, that what they wrote might be received with respect, and deference paid to it: <hi type="italic">It seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us,</hi> that is, to us under the guidance of the Holy Ghost, and by direction from him: not only the apostles, but others, were endued with spiritual gifts extraordinary, and knew more of the mind of God than any since those gifts ceased can pretend to; their infallibility gave an incontestable authority to their decrees, and they would not order any thing because <hi type="italic">it seemed good to them,</hi> but that they knew it first <hi type="italic">seemed good to the Holy Ghost.</hi> Or it refers to what the Holy Ghost had determined in this matter formerly. When the Holy Ghost descended upon the apostles, he endued them with the gift of tongues, in order to their preaching the gospel to the Gentiles, which was a plain indication of God's purpose to call them in. When the Holy Ghost descended upon Cornelius and his friends, upon Peter's preaching, it was plain that Christ designed the taking down of the Jewish pale, within which they fancied the spirit had been enclosed. [2.] They express themselves with abundance of tenderness and fatherly concern. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They are afraid of burdening them: We will <hi type="italic">lay upon you no greater burden.</hi> So far were they from delighting to impose upon them that they dreaded nothing so much as imposing too far upon them, so as to discourage them at their setting out. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They impose upon them <hi type="italic">no other than necessary things.</hi> "The avoiding of <hi type="italic">fornication</hi> is necessary to all Christians at all times; the avoiding of <hi type="italic">things strangled,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">blood,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">things offered to idols,</hi> is necessary at this time, for the keeping up of a good understanding between you and the Jews, and the preventing of offence;" and as long as it continues necessary for that end, and no longer, it is enjoined. Note, Church-rulers should impose only necessary things, things which Christ has made our duty, which have a real tendency to the edification of the church, and, as here, to the uniting of good Christians. If they impose things only to show their own authority, and to try people's obedience, they forget that they have not authority to make new laws, but only to see that the laws of Christ be duly executed, and to enforce the observance of them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They enforce their order with a commendation of those that shall comply with it, rather than with the condemnation of those that shall transgress it. They do not conclude, "From which if you do not keep yourselves, you shall be an anathema, you shall be cast out of the church, and accursed," according to the style of after-councils, and particularly that of Trent; but "<hi type="italic">From which if you keep yourselves,</hi> as we do not question but you will, <hi type="italic">you will do well;</hi> it will be for the glory of God, the furtherance of the gospel, the strengthening of the hands of your brethren, and your own credit and comfort." It is all sweetness and love and good humour, such as became the followers of him who, when he called us to take his yoke upon us, assured us we should find him <hi type="italic">meek and lowly in heart.</hi> The difference of the style of the true apostles from that of the false is very observable. Those that were for imposing the ceremonial laws were positive and imperious: <hi type="italic">Except you keep it, you cannot be saved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.1">v. 1</reference>), you are excommunicated <hi type="italic">ipso facto—at once, and delivered to Satan.</hi> The apostles of Christ, who only recommend necessary things, are mild and gentle: "<hi type="italic">From which if you keep yourselves, you will do well,</hi> and as becomes you. <hi type="italic">Fare ye well;</hi> we are hearty well-wishers to your honour and peace." <div eID="gen29690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29691" type="x-p"/> III. The delivering of the letters, and how the messengers disposed of themselves. <div eID="gen29691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29692" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">When they were dismissed,</hi> had had their audience of leave of the apostles (it is probable that they were dismissed with prayer, and a solemn blessing in the name of the Lord, and with instructions and encouragements in their work), <hi type="italic">They then came to Antioch;</hi> they staid no longer at Jerusalem than till their business was done, and then came back, and perhaps were met at their return by those that brought them on their way at their setting out; for those that have taken pains in public service ought to be countenanced and encouraged. <div eID="gen29692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29693" type="x-p"/> 2. As soon as they came to Antioch, <hi type="italic">they gathered the multitude together, and delivered the epistle to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.30-Acts.15.31">v. 30, 31</reference>), that they might all know what it was that was forbidden them, and might observe these orders, which would be no difficulty for them to do, most of them having been, before their conversion to Christ, proselytes of the gate, who had laid themselves under these restrictions already. But this was not all; it was that they might know that <hi type="italic">no more</hi> than this was forbidden them, that it was no longer a sin to eat swine's flesh, no longer a pollution to touch a grave or a dead body. <div eID="gen29693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29694" type="x-p"/> 3. The people were wonderfully pleased with the orders that came from Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">They rejoiced for the consolation;</hi> and a great consolation it was to the multitude, (1.) That they were confirmed in their freedom from the yoke of the ceremonial law, and were not burdened with that, as those upstart teachers would have had them to be. It was a comfort to them to hear that the carnal ordinances were no longer imposed on them, which perplexed the conscience, but could not purify nor pacify it. (2.) That those who troubled their minds with an attempt to force circumcision upon them were hereby for the present silenced and put to confusion, the fraud of their pretensions to an apostolical warrant being now discovered. (3.) That the Gentiles were hereby encouraged to receive the gospel, and those that had received it to adhere to it. (4.) That the peace of the church was hereby restored, and that removed which threatened a division. All this was consolation which they rejoiced in, and blessed God for. <div eID="gen29694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29695" type="x-p"/> 4. They got the strange ministers that came from Jerusalem to give them each a sermon, and more, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.32">v. 32</reference>. Judas and Silas, <hi type="italic">being prophets also themselves,</hi> endued with the Holy Ghost, and called to the work, and being likewise entrusted by the apostles to deliver some things relating to this matter by word of mouth, <hi type="italic">exhorted the brethren with many words,</hi> and <hi type="italic">confirmed them.</hi> Even those that had the constant preaching of Paul and Barnabas, yet were glad of the help of Judas and Silas; the diversity of the gifts of ministers is of use to the church. Observe what is the work of ministers with those that are in Christ. (1.) To confirm them, by bringing them to see more reason both for their faith in Christ and their obedience to him; to confirm their choice of Christ and their resolutions for Christ. (2.) To exhort them to perseverance, and to the particular duties required of them: to quicken them to that which is good, and direct them in it. They comforted the brethren (so it may be rendered), and this would contribute to the confirming of them; for the joy of the Lord will be our strength. They exhorted them with many words; they used a very great copiousness and variety of expression. One word would affect one, and another another; and therefore, though what they had to say might have been summed up in a few words, yet it was for the edification of the church that they used <hi type="italic">many words,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dia logou pollou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">with much speech, much reasoning; precept must be upon precept.</hi> <div eID="gen29695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29696" type="x-p"/> 5. The dismission of the Jerusalem ministers, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.33">v. 33</reference>. When they had <hi type="italic">spent some time among them</hi> (so it might be read), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">poiesantes chronon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">having made some stay,</hi> and having made it to good purpose, not having trifled away time, but having filled it up, they were let go in peace from the brethren at Antioch, to the apostles at Jerusalem, with all possible expressions of kindness and respect; they thanked them for their coming and pains, and the good service they had done, wished them their health and a good journey home, and committed them to the custody of the peace of God. <div eID="gen29696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29697" type="x-p"/> 6. The continuance of Silas, notwithstanding, together with Paul and Barnabas, at Antioch. (1.)
